newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Court upholds Kalanke reverse discrimination judgment.
newsitem.headline: Court upholds Kalanke reverse discrimination judgment.

text.p: Advocate General Francis Jacobs of the European Court of Justice issued an opinion on Thursday which reconfirmed the end to preferential hiring of women in Germany.

Jacobs reconfirmed the Kalanke case which found that any rule granting women absolute and unconditional priority for appointment or promotion in the workplace is discriminatory and goes beyond promoting equal opportunities.

The Kalanke case was the first European-wide case dealing with issues of reverse discrimination. Members of the European Parliament criticized the case for setting back the progress women have made to reach equal representation in the workplace.

Jacobs told the court that any national rules which give women priority for a higher grade position merely because there are fewer women currently employed in that category, should be struck down as discriminatory.

In a statement issued from the court, the Advocate General denied that the issue was one of reverse discrimination, and said it would be inappropriate if that issue were raised, as that is a policy issue to be determined by legislative bodies.

Instead, Jacobs said the case asks only if German national rules promoting the hiring of women conflict with European Union legislation governing equal treatment in the workplace between men and women.

Under the rules of the European Court, Advocate Generals submit reasoned impartial opinions to the judges to assist them in decision-making. The opinion is not binding and is not a preliminary ruling. However, in a large majority of cases, the reasoning of the opinion is adopted.
